What's the difference between 'administratively down' and 'down/down'?

Administratively down: someone configured shutdown.
Down/down: not shut, but no working link (no cable, far end down, bad cable, speed mismatch).
Right after you configure an IP on a router interface, show ip interface brief shows it 'administratively down / down'. Why?
Router interfaces ship shut down. Configuring an IP doesn't turn the interface on; it still needs no shutdown.
Out of the box, which ports on a new switch are shut down? On a new router?

Switch: none. Ports are enabled and show down/down until something's plugged in.
Router: every interface is administratively down until no shutdown.
An interface shows up/down: status up, protocol down. What does that mean?
Layer 1 is up, but the Layer 2 protocol isn't. Rare on Ethernet; on serial links the classic causes are an encapsulation or keepalive mismatch between the two ends.
A switch port shows err-disabled. What does that mean, and how do you bring it back by hand?

The switch shut the port itself after detecting a problem, like a security violation or repeated flapping.
Fix the cause, then shutdown and no shutdown on the interface.
Input errors 500, CRC 500. What does that tell you?
Every input error is a corrupted frame. Think cabling or interference, or this being the full-duplex side of a duplex mismatch.
Input errors are climbing, but CRC is 0. What does that tell you?
Input errors is a total. With CRC at 0, the errors are coming from its other parts: giants, runts, overruns, and so on. Check those counters.
Why does show interfaces report CRC errors only on the input side?
The sender just attaches the checksum. Only the receiver can recalculate it and compare. Once a frame leaves, the sender can't know what happened to it.
Both ends of a link are confirmed full duplex, but CRC errors keep climbing. Where do you look?
Layer 1: the cable first, then interference, a bad port, or a bad NIC or optic.
A router has been up two years. 'Last clearing of show interface counters: never', CRC 4,312. A user complains about slowness today. Next step?
clear counters on that interface, wait, and check whether CRC is still climbing. Counters add up since boot, so 4,312 could be ancient history.
txload 243/255, rxload 12/255, no error counters increasing. Users say the internet is slow. What's going on?
The outbound direction is about 95% busy. Real congestion, not a fault. txload is traffic this interface sends.
rxload 251/255, txload 30/255, reliability 255/255. What's going on?
Inbound traffic has the link nearly saturated. Reliability 255/255 means no errors, so it's a capacity problem, not a fault.
reliability 190/255 on an interface. Good or bad?
Bad. 255/255 is perfect. 190/255 means a meaningful share of frames are hitting errors. Check the error counters.
What does the bandwidth command on an interface actually change?
Only the number used in calculations like OSPF cost. The link's real speed doesn't change.
An admin sets bandwidth 10000 on a 100 Mbps router interface to limit it to 10 Mbps. What actually happens?
Nothing changes on the wire; the link still runs at 100. Only routing calculations (like OSPF cost) see the new value, so it can change which way traffic is routed.
Interface resets keep climbing on a port. What does that suggest?
The interface keeps going down and back up, usually because of errors underneath: a duplex mismatch, a bad cable, or a failing NIC. Users experience it as random disconnects.
show ip interface Gi0/0 vs show interfaces Gi0/0: what's the difference?

'ip' in the command means the Layer 3 view: addressing and IP settings.
show interfaces is the physical/Layer 2 view: status, MAC, speed, duplex, load, counters.
Which command gives one line per interface with IP address, status, and protocol?
show ip interface brief
On a switch, which command shows each port's status, VLAN, duplex, and speed on one line?
show interfaces status
Write a filter that shows every interface's status line plus its duplex/speed line.

show interfaces | include line protocol|duplex
The | inside the include means OR. No spaces around it, and it's case-sensitive.
show interfaces | include line duplex|speed returns only duplex lines, with no interface names. Why?
The pattern is two phrases: 'line duplex' OR 'speed'. 'line duplex' never appears, and 'speed' only matches the duplex lines through 'Auto-speed'.
What does GigabitEthernet0/1/2 tell you about where the port lives?
slot/subslot/port: slot 0, subslot 1, port 2. On modular routers, 0/0/x is usually built in, and 0/1/x or 0/2/x are module bays. Same idea as Juniper's ge-0/1/2 (FPC/PIC/port).
Why shut a port before applying a lot of config, then bring it up once at the end?
IOS applies every line the moment you press Enter. Some changes bounce the port, and repeated flapping can err-disable it. Shutting first is IOS's stand-in for a Junos commit.
You hardcode speed and duplex on a busy switch port during business hours. What will users see?
A brief outage. Changing speed or duplex bounces the interface.
